title: Trojan Horse
wiki_lead:
In Greek mythology, the Trojan Horse (Greek: δούρειος ἵππος, romanized: doureios hippos, lit. 'wooden horse') was a wooden horse said to have been used by the Greeks during the Trojan War to sneak into the city of Troy and win the war. The Trojan Horse is not mentioned in Homer's Iliad, with the poem ending before the war is concluded, and it is only briefly mentioned in the Odyssey. It is described at length in the Aeneid, in which Virgil recounts how, after a fruitless ten-year siege, the Greeks constructed a huge wooden horse at the behest of Odysseus, and hid a select force of men inside, including Odysseus himself.
The Greeks pretended to sail away, and the Trojans pulled the horse into their city as a victory trophy. That night, the Greek force crept out of the horse and opened the gates for the rest of the Greek army, which had sailed back under the cover of darkness. The Greeks entered and destroyed the city, ending the war. Metaphorically, a "Trojan horse" has come to mean any trick or stratagem that causes a target to invite a foe into a securely protected bastion or place. A malicious computer program that tricks users into willingly running it is also called a "Trojan horse" or simply a "Trojan".
The main ancient source for the story still extant is the Aeneid of Virgil, a Latin epic poem from the time of Augustus. The story featured heavily in the Little Iliad and the Sack of Troy, both part of the Epic Cycle, but these have only survived in fragments and epitomes. As Odysseus was the chief architect of the Trojan Horse, it is also referred to in Homer's Odyssey.
In the Greek tradition, the horse is called the "wooden horse" (δουράτεος ἵππος douráteos híppos in Homeric/Ionic Greek (Odyssey 8.512); δούρειος ἵππος, doúreios híppos in Attic Greek). In Dictys Cretensis' account, the idea of the Trojan Horse's construction comes from Helenus, who prophesies that the Greeks must dedicate a wooden horse to Athena.

Warriors in the horse
Thirty of the Achaeans' best warriors hid in the Trojan horse's womb and two spies in its mouth. Other sources give different numbers: The Bibliotheca 50; Tzetzes 23; and Quintus Smyrnaeus gives the names of 30, but says there were more. In late tradition, the number was standardized at 40. grok_lead: The Trojan Horse is a legendary giant wooden horse from Greek mythology, devised as a stratagem by the Greeks during the Trojan War to infiltrate the fortified city of Troy and secure victory after a decade-long siege. According to Homer's Odyssey, the Greeks constructed the hollow horse under the supervision of Odysseus, concealing elite warriors inside its belly, then pretended to abandon the campaign by sailing away and leaving the structure as an apparent votive offering to the gods. The Trojans, interpreting the Greek withdrawal as a sign of defeat and the horse as a religious giftâpossibly to Athena âhauled it within their walls. In later accounts, this occurred despite warnings from figures like LaocoÃ¶n. That night, the hidden soldiers emerged, opened the city gates, and signaled the returning Greek fleet to storm and sack Troy, ending the war. The tale originates in ancient Greek literature, with its earliest detailed account in Book 8 of Homer's Odyssey (circa 8th century BCE), where the blind poet Demodocus sings of the horse during a banquet on the island of Scheria, emphasizing Odysseus 's cunning role in its creation and the ensuing destruction. The horse was reportedly built by the craftsman Epeius, with Odysseus leading the warriors concealed within, including notable figures like Neoptolemus and Menelaus. While the Iliad focuses on the war's earlier events, the Odyssey and later epic cycles, such as the Little Iliad and Sack of Ilion attributed to other poets in the Epic Cycle, expand on the horse as the decisive ruse that fulfilled prophecies and divine interventions in the conflict. Theories based on archaeological findings at Hisarlik (ancient Troy) propose that the story may symbolize Bronze Age events like earthquakes or represent siege engines, though its core remains mythological. Culturally, the Trojan Horse symbolizes deception, strategic ingenuity, and the perils of hubris, influencing art from ancient Greek pottery depictions of its transport to Roman mosaics and Renaissance paintings. Its narrative has permeated Western literature and drama, as seen in Euripides ' Trojan Women (415 BCE), which explores the aftermath's tragedy, and Virgil's Aeneid (1st century BCE), which adapts it from a Roman perspective. In modern contexts, the term "Trojan horse" denotes any deceptive ploy that undermines from within, extending to cybersecurity where malware disguised as benign software is named after the myth. The story's enduring legacy underscores themes of war's moral costs and the triumph of intellect over brute force.
